lead: This unit explains how a petrol engine makes a spark at the right instant, how a car lights its way and shows the driver what is happening, and how small electric motors and coded keys do the everyday jobs. After it you can read a coil ignition circuit, size a lamp circuit, calculate dwell, spark rate and wiper speed, and explain how an immobiliser stops a stolen car from starting.
about: The unit starts at the battery-and-coil ignition circuit and the physics of the spark, then looks inside the spark plug to work out the voltage and energy a spark needs. Electronic and programmed ignition replace the contact breaker with a transistor and a stored advance map, and distributorless and direct ignition remove the distributor altogether. The unit then turns to light: the light sources and lamp units, the front, rear, interior and special-purpose lamps fed by them, and the adaptive headlamps that level and steer the beam. It closes with the instrument cluster and head-up display, and with the wipers, washers, horns, keyless entry and immobiliser that a driver uses every day.

chapters.idea: A low-voltage primary circuit is interrupted at the right moment, and the collapsing magnetic field in the same coil generates the high voltage that jumps the plug gap.
chapters.depth: Cover the four jobs of an ignition system: generate high voltage, distribute it to the correct cylinder, fire at the correct time, and vary timing with speed and load. Then the battery-and-coil circuit: battery, ignition switch, ballast resistor, primary winding, contact breaker points, capacitor, secondary winding, distributor cap and rotor, spark plugs. Explain mutual induction and the collapse of primary current as the source of the secondary voltage. Define dwell angle and dwell time, and show why a capacitor across the points both speeds the collapse and stops point burning. Mention the names battery-coil ignition, Kettering system and contact-point ignition. Include spark advance mechanisms: centrifugal advance and vacuum advance, with a simple advance curve.

figure.title: Battery-and-coil ignition circuit
figure.aria: Block diagram of a battery-and-coil ignition: battery, switch and primary winding feed the contact breaker, the secondary winding steps the voltage up, and the distributor sends it to the plugs.

chapters.example: A 4-cylinder, 4-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. The contact breaker dwell is 60% of the spark interval. Find the spark frequency, the spark interval, the dwell angle and the dwell time. Solution: 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s; a 4-cylinder 4-stroke engine sparks twice per revolution, so spark frequency = 50 × 2 = 100 sparks/s. Spark interval = 1/100 = 10 ms. Each cylinder fires once per 720° of crank, so the spark interval is 720/4 = 180° of crank; for a 4-cylinder engine the breaker cam gives one opening per 90° of distributor rotation, i.e. 180° of crank. Dwell angle = 0.60 × 180° = 108° of crank. Dwell time = 0.60 × 10 ms = 6 ms.
chapters.trap: Students take rpm/60 as the spark frequency and forget the ×2 for a 4-stroke, or take 60% of 360° instead of 60% of the cylinder angle. Dwell is a fraction of the angle between two sparks, not of a full turn.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the battery, the ignition switch and high-voltage wiring.
chapters.leave: Battery construction and charging to Unit 1; spark plug construction to Chapter 2.2; timing control by the ECU to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A spark plug needs a definite voltage to break down its gap, and that voltage depends on gap size, compression pressure and electrode temperature.
chapters.depth: Spark plug construction: terminal, insulator, centre electrode, ground electrode, suppressor seal, shell, heat range. Explain heat range and why a hot plug suits a cold engine and a cold plug a hot engine. Plug gap, plug fouling, and electrode materials. Then spark pulse generation: the firing voltage needed rises with gap and with cylinder pressure, so the coil must have enough turns ratio and stored energy. Define the high-voltage circuit path from coil secondary through the distributor to the plug and back to earth, and the sources of secondary loss (rotor gap, cable resistance, suppressor caps). Give the standard numbers: firing voltages of about 10–30 kV, plug gaps of 0.7–1.1 mm, spark duration of about 1–2 ms.

figure.aria: Two straight lines show firing voltage rising with spark gap, with the full-load line lying above the light-load line for every gap.

chapters.example: A coil has primary inductance 8 mH and the primary current reaches 6 A before the points open. Find the energy stored. The coil has a 1:100 turns ratio and the primary voltage at break is 250 V. Find the secondary voltage and check whether it fires a plug that needs 22 kV at a 0.9 mm gap on full load. Solution: energy = ½ L I² = 0.5 × 0.008 × 6² = 0.144 J = 144 mJ. Secondary voltage = 100 × 250 V = 25 kV. From the figure at gap 0.9 mm the full-load requirement is 10 + 2.2 × 9 = 29.8 kV, so 25 kV is not enough and the engine will misfire under load; the gap must be reduced or the coil energy raised.
chapters.trap: Multiplying the turns ratio by the battery voltage (12 V) instead of by the voltage actually induced in the primary when the current collapses. The battery voltage never appears across the secondary.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the coil and the primary circuit.
chapters.leave: Knock sensing and spark timing maps to Unit 3 and Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An electronic module or the engine ECU switches the coil current, so dwell and spark timing become computed values that can be programmed against speed, load and temperature.
chapters.depth: Why the contact breaker was replaced: point burning, dwell drift, no timing at high speed. Cover the electronic ignition with a transistor switch and a magnetic or Hall pick-up in place of the points, and dwell control (constant energy, constant dwell). Then programmed ignition, also called electronic spark advance or digital ignition: a look-up map of spark advance against engine speed and manifold pressure, with corrections for coolant temperature, knock and starting. Show the block chain from sensors to ECU to igniter to coil. Mention ignition control methodologies at block level only: mechanical, electronic, mapped, closed-loop with knock retard.

figure.title: Programmed ignition chain
figure.aria: Block diagram of programmed ignition: crank and knock sensors feed the ECU, which drives the ignition driver, coil, distributor and plugs in a single downward chain.

chapters.example: A 4-cylinder 4-stroke engine runs at 5000 rpm and the ignition system holds a dwell of 60%. Find the spark period, the dwell time and the spark advance in milliseconds for a 4° knock retard. Solution: 5000 rpm = 83.33 rev/s; sparks per second = 83.33 × 2 = 166.7; spark period = 1/166.7 = 6 ms. Dwell time = 0.60 × 6 ms = 3.6 ms. One revolution takes 60/5000 s = 12 ms and covers 360°, so 4° of crank takes 4 × 12/360 = 0.133 ms.
chapters.trap: Treating dwell as a fixed angle at all speeds. With constant dwell angle the dwell time shrinks as speed rises and the coil may not reach full current; constant-energy systems hold dwell time instead.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2; crank position sensors from Unit 3.
chapters.leave: The full advance map, knock control loops and fuel interaction to Unit 4; sensor construction to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Each plug, or each pair of plugs, gets its own coil fired by the ECU, so the distributor and its rotor disappear.
chapters.depth: Shorter treatment; only a few universities teach this. Distributorless ignition (also called waste spark ignition): one coil per pair of cylinders, the pair fired together, one spark on compression and one on exhaust. Coil-on-plug and coil-near-plug direct ignition: one coil per cylinder, fired only on compression, triggered by the ECU from crank and cam position. Cover the trigger wheel and the 720° cycle needed to tell compression from exhaust. Advantages: no rotor, no high-voltage cables, better timing accuracy, no wear.

figure.aria: Timeline of one 720 degree cycle showing coil 1 and 4 firing at 0 and 360 degrees and coil 2 and 3 firing at 180 and 540 degrees, in firing order 1-3-4-2.

chapters.example: A 4-cylinder engine with firing order 1-3-4-2 runs at 4000 rpm on a waste-spark system with coils paired 1&4 and 2&3. Find the sparks per second per coil and the crank angle of each spark in the 720° cycle. Solution: 4000 rpm = 66.67 rev/s; total sparks = 66.67 × 2 = 133.3 per second; each coil fires 133.3/2 = 66.7 times per second. The cycle lasts 720° = 2 revolutions = 30 ms. Cylinder 1 fires at 0°, cylinder 3 at 180°, cylinder 4 at 360° and cylinder 2 at 540°. Coil 1&4 sparks at 0° (cylinder 1 compression, cylinder 4 exhaust) and at 360° (cylinder 4 compression, cylinder 1 exhaust).
chapters.trap: Forgetting the 720° cycle. A crank sensor alone cannot say which of the two revolutions is compression, so a cam sensor is needed for true direct ignition.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for the driver and the ECU; Unit 3 for crank and cam sensors.
chapters.leave: Coil driver circuits inside the ECU to Unit 4; cam and crank sensor physics to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Every lamp turns electrical power into light with some efficacy in lumens per watt, and halogen, gas-discharge and LED sources differ mainly in that number and in colour.
chapters.depth: Shorter treatment; only a few universities teach this. Physical principles: incandescence, gas discharge and electroluminescence. Define luminous flux (lumen), luminous intensity (candela), illuminance (lux), luminance and efficacy (lm/W). Cover the light sources: tungsten filament, halogen (about 20–30 lm/W), high-intensity discharge or xenon (about 80 lm/W), light-emitting diode (about 90–110 lm/W) and laser. Cover the lamps built from them: reflector, projector, lens, cut-off shield. Cover technical demands: beam pattern, glare to other drivers, warm-up time, life, vibration, cost.

figure.aria: Tree of automotive light sources split into filament, gas discharge and solid state families, with halogen and LED picked out as the common headlamp choices.

chapters.example: A halogen headlamp uses a 55 W bulb giving 1500 lm. An LED headlamp gives 2000 lm for 20 W. The system runs at 13.2 V while charging. Find the efficacy of each and the current each draws. Solution: halogen efficacy = 1500/55 = 27.3 lm/W; LED efficacy = 2000/20 = 100 lm/W. Halogen current = 55/13.2 = 4.17 A; LED current = 20/13.2 = 1.52 A. The LED gives 33% more flux for 2.65 A less current.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the photometric units: lumen is total light output, candela is light in one direction, lux is light falling on a surface. A lamp is not brighter because it has more lumens if they are spread over a wider beam.
chapters.prereq: Basic electrical power P = V I from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: The lamp circuits and switching to Chapter 2.6; the swivelling mechanism to Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: Lamps are grouped by function — front, rear, interior and special — and each group has its own beam pattern, colour, switching circuit and legal requirement.
chapters.depth: Shorter treatment; only a few universities teach this. Front: headlamp main and dip beam, daytime running lamps, fog lamps, position lamps; beam patterns and the asymmetric dip cut-off. Rear: tail, stop, reversing, direction indicator, rear fog, number-plate lamp; colour rules (red to the rear, white or amber to the front). Interior: dome, map, vanity, ambient, boot and glovebox lamps, dimming. Special purpose: hazard warning, beacon and flashing lamps for ambulances and police, work lamps, school-bus lamps. Cover the circuit path: battery, fuse, switch or relay, earth return, and the flasher unit that sets the indicator rate. Mention electric horns as another auxillary load on the same circuit family.

figure.title: Lighting circuit path
figure.aria: Circuit block diagram from battery through fuse, switch and relay to a lamp and earth, with a dashed branch from the switch to the flasher unit and indicator lamps.

chapters.example: A car has two 55 W headlamps, two 5 W tail lamps, two 5 W number-plate lamps and 3 W of instrument illumination on at the same time. The battery is at 12.6 V. Find the total current and choose a fuse rating. Solution: total power = 2 × 55 + 2 × 5 + 2 × 5 + 3 = 110 + 10 + 10 + 3 = 133 W. Current = 133/12.6 = 10.6 A. The next standard fuse above this with margin is 15 A, which carries the load and still protects the wiring.
chapters.trap: Adding the wattages and dividing by 12 V when the alternator is charging at 13.8–14.4 V, which gives a current that is too high; and forgetting that the brake lamps add 42 W only when the pedal is pressed.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 for the lamp types and their ratings.
chapters.leave: Alternator output and battery capacity to Unit 1; adaptive headlamps to Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: Adaptive lighting moves the beam with the steering and keeps it level with the road, using sensors, a small motor and an ECU rather than a fixed lamp housing.
chapters.depth: Shorter treatment; only a few universities teach this. Adaptive front lighting system (AFS): swivel or bending light that turns the headlamp with steering angle and vehicle speed, and leveling that corrects pitch from load. Cover the inputs (steering angle sensor, vehicle speed, ride height sensor, camera), the actuator (stepper or DC motor with a position sensor) and the limits that stop glare above about 15°. Mention adaptive driving beam and matrix LED, where individual LED segments switch off to shade oncoming traffic. Keep the control explanation at block level.

figure.title: Adaptive headlamp control
figure.aria: Block diagram where steering angle, speed and camera inputs reach the adaptive lighting ECU, which drives a swivel motor and a level motor that both move the headlamp.

chapters.example: A 75 kg load in the boot sinks the rear of the car by 20 mm. The headlamp sits 2.0 m ahead of the rear axle. Find the pitch angle and the levelling correction. Separately, the steering wheel is turned 90°, the steering ratio is 16:1 and the swivel command is 0.15 × steering wheel angle, capped at 15°. Find the swivel angle. Solution: tan θ = 20/2000 = 0.010, so θ = 0.57°; the beam tilts up by 0.57° and the level motor must tilt the lamp down by 0.57°. Road wheel angle = 90/16 = 5.6°. Swivel command = 0.15 × 90 = 13.5°, which is below the 15° cap, so the lamp turns 13.5°.
chapters.trap: Confusing levelling with swivelling. Levelling corrects pitch (up-down) from load and braking; swivelling corrects yaw (left-right) from steering. A car can have one without the other.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.5 and 2.6 for the lamp and its beam; steering angle sensors from Unit 3.
chapters.leave: Camera image processing and driver assistance functions to Unit 5; sensor construction to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The instrument cluster is a small computer on the bus: it receives frames from other ECUs, converts them into needle, digit or projected image, and warns the driver.
chapters.depth: Cover the cluster as a display system: speedometer, tachometer, fuel and temperature gauges, odometer, telltales, warning lamps, driver information display. Explain how speed is derived from wheel pulses or gearbox pulses (pulses per kilometre, distance per pulse). Cover the stepper-motor needle drive, the LCD and TFT panel, and the dimming and self-test functions. Then the head-up display: combiner or windscreen projection, virtual image distance, why the image is focused far ahead to keep the driver's eyes on the road. Cover cluster messages on CAN, and simple fault indication. Mention that the cluster also stores and shows fault codes.

figure.aria: Sequence of messages over time: the wheel sensor and engine ECU send data to the cluster, the cluster shows needle and head-up display information to the driver, and the driver sends a dimming command back.

chapters.example: A speedometer receives 4 pulses per wheel revolution and the tyre rolling circumference is 1.90 m. Find the distance per pulse, the pulse frequency at 100 km/h and the number of pulses counted in a 0.5 s sampling window. Solution: distance per pulse = 1.90/4 = 0.475 m. 100 km/h = 100/3.6 = 27.78 m/s. Wheel revolutions per second = 27.78/1.90 = 14.62; pulse frequency = 14.62 × 4 = 58.5 pulses/s. Pulses in 0.5 s = 58.5 × 0.5 = 29.2, so the counter reads 29 and the cluster scales it to about 97 km/h for that window; averaging over several windows removes the error.
chapters.trap: Assuming the speedometer is driven directly by engine rpm. It is driven by wheel or gearbox pulses, so tyre size and final drive ratio change the reading, and a wheel-speed signal is also what ABS uses.
chapters.prereq: Basic CAN frame ideas from Unit 6; speed sensing from Unit 3.
chapters.leave: CAN frame format and OBD-II to Unit 6; ABS wheel-speed processing to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Small electric motors wipe the screen and wash it, and a coded two-way conversation between the key and the car decides whether the engine is allowed to start.
chapters.depth: Wiper and washer system: wiper motor with permanent magnet and two or three brushes for high and low speed, the park switch that stops the blade at the bottom, the intermittent relay, the washer pump and the rain sensor. Then keyless entry: remote keyless entry with a radio fob and rolling code, and passive keyless entry where a proximity handshake unlocks the door. Then the immobiliser: transponder in the key, coil around the lock barrel, challenge-response, and the engine ECU refusing to fire the plugs or open the injectors if the code does not match. Mention electric horns and central locking as related body loads.

figure.aria: Sequence diagram of an immobiliser handshake: the key fob sends a rolling code to the receiver, the immobiliser ECU validates it, sends a start enable to the engine ECU, receives a running confirmation, and advances the rolling counter.

chapters.example: A wiper arm is 500 mm long and sweeps through 120°. It completes 45 wipes per minute. The intermittent delay uses a 100 kΩ resistor and a 100 µF capacitor. Find the wiper tip speed and the delay time. Solution: 120° = 2.094 rad; arc per sweep = 0.5 × 2.094 = 1.047 m. One wipe is out and back = 2 × 1.047 = 2.094 m. 45 wipes/min = 0.75 wipes/s, so tip speed = 0.75 × 2.094 = 1.57 m/s. Delay time = R × C = 100 000 × 0.0001 = 10 s.
chapters.trap: Saying the immobiliser stops the starter motor. On most cars it stops the spark and the injectors, so the engine cranks but never fires; and a rolling code that is out of step will fail even with the correct key.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the battery and starting circuit; Unit 6 for body-network messages.
chapters.leave: Central locking motors and body control details to Unit 6; starting motor circuits to Unit 1.
